h.strategy: Use retrieved findings to judge which settings are strong, weak or neutral, and which parts other settings can cut off from the outcome. Build hypotheses mainly from (a) the edited field's current parent value: replacing a strong value with a weak one hurts, and filling an empty or harmful slot helps; and (b) conditions that disconnect the edited part, pushing its effect toward zero. Directions refer to the signed effect, not its size. Disconnection makes the effect lower only if the edit usually helps, and higher if it usually hurts. If the usual sign is unclear, do not use it. When finding flaws, check this sign logic first. Replace any hypothesis whose direction could reverse through a competing effect or that relies on partial redundancy. Vary edit fields and values. State a one-sentence mechanism.

hyps.why: With edge 0 removed, node 1 has no input, so the edge 2 conv is disconnected and its usual positive effect shrinks.
With node 1 cut off from the input, a conv on edge 4 carries no signal, so its usual gain vanishes.
A conv on edge 4 cannot help when node 1 receives nothing from the input.
Removing a strong conv from the direct edge hurts more than removing a weak op or a no-op.
Removing a 3x3 conv into the output loses more capacity than removing a weak op or an empty edge.
Deleting a strong conv on the final edge costs more than deleting a weak op.
Cutting the first edge when it holds a strong conv removes a major path, which hurts more than cutting a weak op.
Removing a 3x3 conv on the intermediate edge destroys a strong path.
Filling the empty direct input-to-output edge with a strong conv gains more than replacing an existing op.
Turning an empty edge into a 3x3 conv adds a useful path, unlike swapping between non-empty ops.
